context: Retinal vein occlusion (RVO) is a blockage of one or more veins that carry blood away from the retina — the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye — and is the second most common retinal vascular disorder after diabetic retinopathy. Affecting an estimated 16 million people worldwide, RVO usually occurs in people over age 50 and is most often caused by a blood clot or by a hardened retinal artery pressing on a vein at an arteriovenous crossing. The blockage can cause blood and fluid to leak into the retina, leading to macular edema (swelling of the central retina), and in more severe cases the growth of abnormal new blood vessels (neovascularization) that can cause bleeding, retinal detachment, and dangerously elevated eye pressure (neovascular glaucoma). There is no safe way to physically unblock the retinal vein; treatment focuses on managing complications and protecting remaining vision.
subject: Retinal Vein Occlusion (RVO; eye vein occlusion)

types: Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) — blockage of the eye's main retinal vein; may be nonischemic (mild, with leaky retinal vessels) or ischemic (severe, with reduced or blocked blood flow)
Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) — blockage of one of the smaller branch veins draining a section of the retina; more common than CRVO
causes: Blood clot (thrombus) blocking blood flow through the retinal vein — including thrombosis of the central retinal vein posterior to the lamina cribrosa in CRVO

Compression of a retinal vein at an arteriovenous crossing, where a hardened/thickened retinal artery (atherosclerosis) presses on the adjacent vein, causing turbulent flow, endothelial damage, and thrombosis — the principal mechanism of BRVO
Slowdown of blood flow through the retinal vein
Less commonly: inherited or acquired clotting disorders, dysproteinemias, vasculitis, antiphospholipid syndrome, or hyperviscosity syndromes (especially in patients under 40)
symptoms: Blurry or reduced vision — often sudden, in part or all of one eye; can develop over hours or days and may be the only symptom at onset
Floaters — dark spots, lines, or squiggles in the field of vision from blood leaking into the vitreous
Pain or pressure in the affected eye — more typical of severe/ischemic occlusions and of neovascular glaucoma
Sudden, partial (BRVO) or central (CRVO) field-of-vision defect or loss of vision including total loss in severe cases
May be asymptomatic — particularly with small branch occlusions — and detected only on a routine dilated eye exam
risk_factors: Older age (most cases occur in adults aged 50 or older; RVO is uncommon in younger patients)
Cardiovascular disease and elevated body mass index (obesity)
Hypercoagulable states — hyperhomocysteinemia, anticardiolipin antibodies; rarely blood cancers such as lymphoma, leukemia, or multiple myeloma; eye trauma
History of retinal vein occlusion in one eye increases risk for the other eye
treatment_options: Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections — first-line therapy for macular edema and neovascularization; agents include aflibercept (Eylea), bevacizumab (Avastin), ranibizumab (Lucentis/Byooviz/Cimerli/Susvimo), and the bispecific antibody faricimab-svoa (Vabysmo); repeated over months to years as needed

Corticosteroid (steroid) injections or sustained-release implants — second-line option to reduce macular edema when anti-VEGF is insufficient; risks include elevated eye pressure and cataract formation

Laser photocoagulation — focal/grid laser to seal leaking perifoveal vessels (especially in BRVO) and panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) to cause regression of abnormal new vessels in severe ischemic CRVO
Vitrectomy surgery (pars plana vitrectomy) — for persistent vitreous hemorrhage (e.g., bleeding lasting more than four weeks or recurring) or for tractional retinal detachment

Coordination with primary care to control underlying medical risk factors — blood pressure, blood glucose, cholesterol — through diet, exercise, weight, smoking cessation, and medications such as antihypertensives or lipid-lowering drugs

Ongoing monitoring with dilated eye exam, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and fluorescein angiography to detect complications (macular edema, neovascularization, retinal detachment) and guide treatment timing
